**Greece connects IRIS to European instant payments network**

*Greece's IRIS instant payments system has joined the EuroPA network, enabling cross-border euro transfers between Greek banks and counterparts across Europe.*

Greek banks can now send and receive instant payments across borders through the EuroPA interoperability framework, with DIAS S.A. handling the technical connection. Minister Kyriakos Pierrakakis described IRIS as a centrepiece of Greece's digital economy strategy, and the cross-border link adds a practical dimension to that claim.

Greece is a relatively late entrant to cross-border instant payments interoperability, but the timing aligns with the EU's instant payments regulation mandate and broader efforts to build a unified European payments space. Eurobank confirmed it is among the first Greek banks to offer the service.

The move is notable less for Greece's individual weight in European payment volumes than for the pattern it represents. Each new market joining cross-border instant payment networks raises the baseline expectation for coverage, making holdouts more conspicuous and strengthening the case for schemes such as Wero that depend on pan-European reach.

*Sources: [IRIS Payments connects Greece with European EuroPA network](https://thepaypers.com/payments/news/iris-payments-connects-greece-with-european-europa-network) — The Paypers | [Pierrakakis: IRIS is the success story of the Greek digital economy](https://en.protothema.gr/2026/06/30/pierrakakis-iris-is-the-success-story-of-the-greek-digital-economy/) — ProtoThema | [Eurobank: Digital payments and cross-border money transfers in the EU via IRIS](https://www.euro2day.gr/en2/article/2358163/eurobank-digital-payments-and-crossborder-money-tr) — Euro2day*

stories.original:
**Visa, Mastercard and Google back Open USD stablecoin launch**

*A consortium of major payment networks, banks and technology firms is backing Open USD, a new stablecoin that positions card schemes as participants in, rather than bystanders to, the tokenised money ecosystem.*

Visa, Mastercard, US Bank, Google and Coinbase are among dozens of firms supporting Open USD, which is expected to launch later this year. The breadth of the backing group is striking: it spans card networks, a major issuing bank, a crypto-native exchange and a platform company, suggesting an attempt to build a stablecoin with broad commercial acceptance from launch rather than relying on organic adoption.

The announcement follows Mastercard's recent move to add stablecoin settlement to its merchant network, and sits alongside Tether's expanding footprint in emerging markets. For European observers, the relevant question is whether Open USD accelerates demand for a euro-denominated equivalent, or whether US-dollar stablecoins continue to dominate by default. The digital euro project and private initiatives such as AllUnity's planned Swedish krona stablecoin are both attempting to answer that question, but neither is yet in production.

The involvement of both Visa and Mastercard is particularly worth watching. Both networks have historically competed to own the rails; co-sponsoring a shared stablecoin suggests they see tokenised settlement as a layer where collaboration is more valuable than rivalry.

*Sources: [Big payment names back new stablecoin](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48017/big-payment-names-back-new-stablecoin) — Finextra*

stories.original:
**Pay.UK introduces flexible liquidity model for Faster Payments access**

*Pay.UK has launched a new net sender cap model for Faster Payments, lowering liquidity barriers for smaller and newer participants joining the UK's core instant payments infrastructure.*

The new model introduces flexibility in how participants fund their net sender caps, replacing a more rigid structure that effectively set a higher floor for participation. Pay.UK framed the change as a way to widen access to Faster Payments for a broader range of firms.

The timing matters. The UK Payments Initiative is building a new domestic scheme intended to challenge card networks, and its viability depends partly on the breadth of firms connected to core payment rails. Lowering the cost of Faster Payments participation makes it easier for smaller banks, payment institutions and e-money firms to connect directly rather than relying on agency arrangements with larger banks.

Liquidity management has become a persistent theme across European instant payments, with the SEPA instant payments mandate forcing banks to rethink prefunding and intraday liquidity. Pay.UK's move addresses the same underlying tension: real-time payment systems require real-time liquidity, and rigid capital requirements can exclude the firms most likely to drive innovation at the edges of the network.

*Sources: [Pay.UK launches liquidity model for faster payments](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110304/payuk-launches-liquidity-model-for-faster-payments) — Finextra*

**CFPB rewrites US open banking rule with narrower data scope and new fees**

*The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has substantially revised its open banking rule, limiting the data companies can access and introducing fees for data sharing, in a shift that narrows the scope of US open finance before it begins.*

The rewritten rule scales back the range of data that third parties can request from banks, and for the first time allows financial institutions to charge for API access. Both changes represent a significant departure from the original rule finalised under the Biden administration, which drew heavily on the UK and EU model of free, broad data access.

For European firms with US operations or ambitions, the practical effect is a more constrained US open banking environment than many had anticipated. The fee mechanism in particular diverges from the European approach, where ASPSP access has been provided without charge. Fintechs relying on comprehensive account data for affordability, verification or payment initiation will need to adjust their US product strategies.

The revision also complicates any future push toward reciprocal data-sharing arrangements between the US and Europe. The BIS's recent Project Aperta prototype for cross-border open finance interoperability assumed broadly comparable data access regimes; a US framework built on narrower data rights and paid access introduces friction that technical standards alone cannot resolve.

*Sources: [CFPB rewrites US open banking rule with data limits and fintech fees](https://www.google.com/url?rct=j&sa=t&url=https://washingtonreporter.news/exclusive-rep-pat-harrigan-homes-in-on-foreign-fraud-with-latest-legislation/) — previously covered June 30*
